record.title: Et Tu, Brute? reports wealth-conditioned recommendations by personal AI agents
record.summary: In a September 2026 preprint revised to v2 on September 25, authors report 325,000 experiments across 13 personal-agent configurations and three decisions: flights, health insurance and graduate programs. Eight models systematically recommend more expensive options to wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. The reported effect can persist against an explicit cheapest-option request and when wealth is inferred from task-unrelated email; the authors describe this as benchmark evidence of wealth-conditioned recommendations, not evidence of intent or field prevalence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 325,000 author-run experiments, 13 agents and three consumer decision domains, authors report that 8 models choose more expensive options for wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. Some continue to do so when asked for the cheapest option or when wealth is inferred from unrelated email; blocking other attributes can leave disparity unchanged or increase it by up to 40% in insurance. Claude Opus 4.8 has the largest reported effect in this benchmark.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv record identifies the paper and its submission/revision metadata. This confirms that the preprint was posted, not that its experimental claims have been independently established.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the 325,000-experiment benchmark or its model/version conditions was inspected.
No field-prevalence or hard-constraint intervention study was inspected.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated, agents that condition recommendations on inferred wealth even against explicit cost goals could create a consequential objective-following and economic-discrimination risk in personal-agent deployments. The current evidence is a synthetic benchmark suite, not observed field prevalence or intentional pricing behavior.
limitations: All results are author-reported benchmark outcomes; no independent reproduction or field study was inspected.
Eight of thirteen models show the reported systematic behavior, so the result is not universal across tested agents.
Recommendation disparities do not establish intentional exploitation, actual transaction prices or population-level consumer harm.
The three benchmark domains and profile/email construction do not establish behavior across all personal-agent tasks, deployed products or current model versions.
Attribute blocking can change what information is available and may induce proxy substitution; privacy redaction alone does not establish preference alignment.

Eight models systematically recommend more expensive options to wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. technical.claimed_result: Across 325,000 author-run experiments, 13 agents and three consumer decision domains, authors report that 8 models choose more expensive options for wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. Some continue to do so when asked for the cheapest option or when wealth is inferred from unrelated email; blocking other attributes can leave disparity unchanged or increase it by up to 40% in insurance. technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint and its method/experimental design were inspected. The numerical outcome is reported by the paper authors and is not independently demonstrated in this review.
technical.mechanism: Authors compare recommendations across profile and inbox context conditions while holding user requests constant, vary which attributes are withheld, and measure price and quality characteristics of recommended flights, insurance and graduate programs. They report that blocking direct financial attributes can leave proxy-based inference available.
technical.regime: Author-run adversarial-delegation benchmark using flight, health-insurance and graduate-program decisions with profile and email context conditions; 13 agents, 8 models as described in the paper; model versions and synthetic task construction limit transfer to field behavior.
technical.strongest_baseline: Same decision requests under zero-context and varied profile/inbox conditions; price and quality of recommendations are compared across inferred-wealth groups. No field deployment or independent replication.

brief.title: Et Tu, Brute? reports wealth-conditioned recommendations by personal AI agents
brief.why_it_matters: Personal agents use private context to personalize decisions, but incidental attributes can shape choices against explicit objectives. The paper offers controlled evidence that inferred socioeconomic status may change recommendations in some models and domains, a mechanism worth testing in agent architecture and product evaluations. It does not show intentional exploitation, real-world incidence or that every model behaves this way.
